content: 1. Inform the patient that HIV testing will be conducted routinely, similar to other blood tests, but emphasize that she has the right to decline the test. 2. Ask the patient if she has been tested for HIV before. If she has not been tested, explain that she will be tested unless she refuses. If she has been tested, review the results and clarify that she is not obligated to disclose them. 3. Inquire if the patient is currently taking any antiretroviral (ARV) medications and review her ARV treatment plan if applicable. 4. Ask if her partner has been tested for HIV and check the records for confirmation. 5. Determine when the patient was last tested for HIV during this pregnancy, particularly if it was in the first trimester. 6. If the HIV test result is positive: Initiate appropriate antiretroviral therapy (ART) and provide counseling on adherence to the treatment. Discuss the implications of a positive test result and refer her to specialized HIV services for further assessment and lifelong ART initiation. Offer additional care and support tailored to HIV-infected women, including counseling on disclosure, partner testing, safer sex practices (e.g., condom use), family planning, and infant feeding options. Schedule her for the next antenatal care visit. 7. If the HIV test result is negative: Counsel her on the importance of maintaining her negative status by practicing safer sex, including consistent condom use. Encourage partner testing and repeat HIV testing in the third trimester. 8. If the patient refuses the HIV test or does not disclose her previous test results: Assess for signs of severe or advanced HIV infection, such as weight loss, chronic diarrhea, prolonged fever, persistent cough, or difficulty breathing. Counsel her on safer sex practices and the benefits of partner testing. 9. For pregnant women with unknown HIV status or signs of advanced infection, refer them to a clinic or hospital offering advanced treatment services. 10. If the patient reports no fetal movement: Ask when she last felt the baby move and palpate for fetal movements. After six months of pregnancy, listen for the fetal heartbeat. If no fetal movement is detected, inform the patient and her partner about the possibility of fetal demise and refer her to a hospital. 11. If the patient has ruptured membranes without labor: Determine when the membranes ruptured and examine for amniotic fluid or foul-smelling vaginal discharge. If no evidence is found, ask her to wear a pad and recheck in one hour. If fever or signs of infection are present, administer appropriate antibiotics and refer her urgently to a hospital. 12. If the patient has a fever or burning sensation during urination: Measure her temperature and assess for signs of severe febrile illness, such as stiff neck or lethargy. If a severe febrile disease is suspected, initiate IV fluids, antibiotics, antimalarials (if malaria is confirmed), and glucose, and refer her urgently to a hospital. 13. If the patient has a lower urinary tract infection, provide oral antibiotics and encourage increased fluid intake. If no improvement occurs within two days, refer her to a hospital. 14. If the patient has abnormal vaginal discharge: Ask about changes in discharge, vulvar itching, or urinary problems in her partner. Examine for abnormal discharge, noting its amount, color, and odor. Treat possible infections (e.g., gonorrhea, chlamydia, candida, or trichomonas) with appropriate antibiotics or antifungals and counsel on safer sex practices. 15. If the patient has signs of advanced HIV infection but refuses testing: Assess for symptoms such as weight loss, chronic diarrhea, prolonged fever, persistent cough, or difficulty breathing. Look for visible wasting, skin rashes, blisters, enlarged lymph nodes, oral thrush, or abnormal vaginal discharge. Refer her to a clinic or hospital for advanced treatment services. 16. If the patient smokes, uses alcohol or drugs, or has a history of violence: Assess for dependency on tobacco or alcohol and counsel on cessation. Refer her to specialized care providers for substance abuse or violence counseling. 17. If the patient has a cough or difficulty breathing: Determine the duration of symptoms and assess for associated signs such as chest pain, blood in sputum, or wheezing. If pneumonia is suspected, administer the first dose of antibiotics and refer her urgently to a hospital. If chronic lung disease is suspected, refer her for further assessment. 18. If the patient is taking anti-tuberculosis drugs: Confirm the treatment regimen and ensure it does not include streptomycin, which is ototoxic to the fetus. Reassure her that other TB drugs are safe during pregnancy and encourage adherence to treatment. If her sputum is TB-positive within two months of delivery, plan to provide INH prophylaxis to the newborn. 19. Provide preventive measures during antenatal care: Administer tetanus toxoid if due and provide a three-month supply of iron, aspirin, calcium, and ART if prescribed. Counsel on adherence to medications and safety. Encourage sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets and provide intermittent preventive treatment for malaria. 20. Counsel on nutrition and self-care during pregnancy: Advise the patient to eat a variety of healthy foods and avoid harmful taboos. Encourage rest, avoidance of heavy lifting, and safer sex practices. Discourage alcohol and smoking and advise against taking non-prescribed medications. 21. Develop a birth and emergency plan: Discuss labor signs and danger signs requiring immediate medical attention. Advise on facility delivery and review arrangements for transportation, costs, and support during labor. Prepare the patient for home delivery with a skilled attendant if necessary, ensuring she has the required supplies. 22. Counsel on the importance of facility delivery, especially for HIV-infected women, to ensure access to appropriate care and ARV treatment during childbirth. 23. Advise on when to go to the facility based on proximity and what to bring, such as clean clothes, maternal records, and supplies for the baby.
